passage: On the verandah of their house in a Bihar village, Aparna slid the wooden star through its slot, plop, and smiled at her son. "See, Ujjwal?" Ujjwal grabbed a star, held it flat like a biscuit and dropped it on the lid. It bounced off and rolled to the step. He fetched it, climbed back, held it flat again above the box, and let go. Bounce. He frowned and started over.

qa.q: Where did the star roll after it bounced off?
qa.a: It rolled to the step.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal thinking as he dropped the star again?
qa.a: He seemed hopeful that dropping it just like Amma would work, and puzzled and a bit frustrated when it kept bouncing.

qa.q: What else could Aparna show Ujjwal?
qa.a: She could slowly show him how she turns the star upright before dropping it, since he copied the drop but not the angle.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal's copying look to Aparna?
qa.a: She probably finds it sweet and sees that he watched her closely but missed how she held the piece.

grounding: A toddler copies his mother dropping a star into its slot but holds it flat, so it bounces off and he starts again.

passage: Rosa knelt on the kitchen floor of their Lisbon flat and posted the green star into the sorter. "In it goes!" Emeka watched, then snatched another star, held it flat between finger and thumb, and let it fall. It clacked on the lid and skittered away. He crawled after it, came back, lifted it high above the box and dropped it flat again. Clack. He looked at Rosa, then at the star.

qa.q: What colour was the star Rosa posted?
qa.a: It was green.

qa.q: What does Emeka's look at Rosa and then the star suggest?
qa.a: He seems puzzled and a little frustrated, trying to work out why her drop worked and his did not.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Emeka?
qa.a: Turn the star so its points match the hole before he drops it, or guide his hand once, because the angle is what he missed.

qa.q: How might Rosa feel as she watches?
qa.a: Rosa is probably amused and touched that he copies her, and patient as he tries again.

grounding: A toddler copies his mother dropping a star into a sorter but holds it flat, sees it bounce and starts from the top again.

passage: In the courtyard of the house near Sitapur, Vikas sat with the wooden shape board his uncle had made. The square block wouldn't go into the round hole. He smacked it with his palm. Smack. Smack. Smack. His sister Disha, drawing water at the handpump, called, "Vikas, that's the wrong hole!" He smacked harder, face red, the block hopping on the rim and never sinking in.

qa.q: What was Disha doing at the handpump?
qa.a: She was drawing water.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling as he smacked harder?
qa.a: He was frustrated and stubborn, sure that more force would push the block in.

qa.q: What else could Vikas try instead of smacking?
qa.a: He could try the block in the other holes or turn to Disha for help, because hitting harder does not change the block's shape.

qa.q: How does the smacking look to Disha?
qa.a: Disha sees clearly that he has the wrong hole and is a little amused and a little exasperated that he won't listen.

grounding: A toddler hammers a square block on a round hole with his palm, putting in effort that cannot change the fit.

passage: Sami knelt on the living-room carpet in Tunis, a blue square block pressed to the round hole of the shape box. Thump went his palm. Thump. Thump. His father, Siddiq, looked up from folding towels. "Strong hands!" Sami thumped harder, lips pressed together. The block stayed on top, not budging. His palm turned pink. He thumped once more, then shoved the whole box.

qa.q: What was Siddiq doing when he looked up?
qa.a: He was folding towels.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling when he shoved the whole box?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated after all his thumping failed.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Sami better?
qa.a: Trying the block in other holes or turning it to match, since force alone can't change a square into a circle.

qa.q: How might Siddiq see the thumping?
qa.a: Siddiq first sees effort and praises it, then may realise Sami needs a nudge toward the square hole instead.

grounding: A toddler hits a square block on the round hole again and again, and the force changes nothing.

passage: On the wooden floor of their Kottayam home, Jomon pushed a triangle at the triangle hole, but it caught on one edge. He tried twice, then turned and held it up to his amma. His eyes stayed on her face. She turned it a little in her fingers and set it back on the hole. Jomon pushed, and it dropped. He clapped both hands and laughed out loud.

qa.q: Where did the triangle catch?
qa.a: It caught on one edge.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he clapped and laughed?
qa.a: He was delighted and proud that he pushed the block in himself after Amma's small turn.

qa.q: What else could Amma try next time to help him learn?
qa.a: She could turn it slowly while he watches, so he sees the move she made and can try it himself.

qa.q: How does the moment feel for Amma?
qa.a: She gets to help without taking over, and enjoys seeing him finish it and laugh.

grounding: A toddler hands a stuck block to his mother, she turns it slightly, and he pushes it the rest of the way, then claps.

subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage: Zanele's big brother Yosef was watching cartoons in the Durban flat when Zanele toddled past with a stuck circle block. She had tried the hole three times. Now she held it up to Mama and looked at her, waiting. Mama tilted it, just slightly, and gave it back. Zanele pressed it in with one finger. It fell with a thunk. She clapped hard, and Yosef clapped too.

qa.q: Who was watching cartoons?
qa.a: Zanele's big brother Yosef was.

qa.q: How can you tell Zanele felt proud?
qa.a: She clapped hard after pressing the block in herself.

qa.q: What small step helped here, and why?
qa.a: Mama tilted the block only slightly and gave it back, so Zanele could finish the job herself.

qa.q: How might Yosef see his little sister's success?
qa.a: He seems happy for her and joins in, clapping too.

grounding: A toddler hands her mother a stuck block, her mother tilts it slightly, and the toddler pushes it in and claps.

passage: I'm Vasudha, and I run the play corner at the clinic in Kolkata. Arnab had been at the shape box a long while. The oval block kept missing. He turned it, pushed, turned it, pushed. Then he dropped it, shoved the box away with his foot and crawled off to the stacking cups. Was he cross? Tired? I couldn't tell. He built a wobbly cup tower, humming. I kept the box aside for another day.

qa.q: What did Arnab crawl off to?
qa.a: He crawled off to the stacking cups.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she watched Arnab leave the box?
qa.a: Vasudha was curious and unsure whether he was cross or tired, and calm enough to let him go.

qa.q: What went well in Arnab leaving the puzzle?
qa.a: He stopped before tears and turned to something easier, so his mood stayed good and the box can be tried again another day.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel once he is building cups?
qa.a: He seems settled and content, humming as he builds.

grounding: An observer describes a toddler who leaves a puzzle after many failed tries and turns to stacking cups, which keeps his mood intact.

passage:
Tuesday: Bidisha pushed the heart block at every hole, whined, then shoved the sorter away and crawled to her cups. Devika, her mother, let her go.
Thursday: Bidisha stacked cups all morning and never looked at the sorter.
Saturday: she pulled the sorter out herself, found the heart, turned it once and it slid in. She looked up at Devika, eyebrows high.

qa.q: What did Bidisha stack on Thursday?
qa.a: She stacked cups all morning.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling on Saturday when the heart slid in?
qa.a: She was surprised and pleased, looking up at Devika with eyebrows high.

qa.q: Why was letting her walk away on Tuesday a good choice?
qa.a: Leaving the sorter protected her mood, so she came back to it on her own and could solve it.

qa.q: How does Devika see the three days?
qa.a: Devika sees that stepping back let Bidisha return calm and succeed, which is probably reassuring.

grounding: Over several days a toddler leaves a puzzle she cannot solve, plays with cups instead, and later returns and succeeds.

passage:
Note for Chinmay's mother, Alka
Today Chinmay wanted the big sofa. First he flopped tummy-down across the seat and slid off. Then he hooked one knee up and wriggled. Then he rolled sideways and ended up on the floor, giggling. He went back to the knee hook, and this time the knee went over the edge and he hauled himself up. After that he used only the knee. I stayed close throughout.

qa.q: What did Chinmay try first?
qa.a: He flopped tummy-down across the seat and slid off.

qa.q: How can you tell Chinmay felt happy trying?
qa.a: He giggled even when he rolled off onto the floor, and went straight back to try again.

qa.q: What else could the note-writer do to help next time?
qa.a: They could put a firm floor cushion by the sofa as a step, so Chinmay has another option while still working it out himself.

qa.q: How might Alka feel reading this note?
qa.a: Alka would probably feel proud of Chinmay's persistence and reassured that someone stayed close.

grounding: A caregiver's note describes a toddler trying different ways to climb a sofa and keeping the one that gets the knee over the edge.

passage: The new cane sofa had arrived at Dilnaz's house in Malappuram, and Kishore, her toddler, wanted up. He tried lying on his tummy on the seat, legs kicking, then slid off. He tried rolling, and bumped back down. Then he lifted one knee high and hooked it on the edge. It stuck. He pushed, grabbed the cushion and was on. Next go, he went straight for the knee.

qa.q: What had arrived at Dilnaz's house?
qa.a: The new cane sofa had arrived.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when his knee stuck on the edge?
qa.a: He was probably excited and determined, pushing hard once he found a move that worked.

qa.q: What small step would help Kishore climb safely?
qa.a: Dilnaz could stay close while he practises the knee move, so he keeps learning but has someone there if he slips.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see his tries?
qa.a: She sees her toddler testing one way after another and settling on the knee, which may feel impressive and amusing.

grounding: A toddler tries several ways onto the sofa and stays with the one that gets his knee over the edge.

passage:
Home visit note, Wednesday
Parveen watched her big brother come in from school, turn his back to the divan, sit and swing his legs up. She toddled over and turned around too, bumped her back against the edge, then threw one leg up and wriggled. She ended up half on the divan, nearer than any try this week. She lay there panting and grinning. I stood near the edge in case she slipped.

qa.q: Where did Parveen end up?
qa.a: She ended up half on the divan.

qa.q: What does Parveen's panting and grinning suggest?
qa.a: She seems pleased and proud that copying her brother got her further than before.

qa.q: What would you advise the family to try next?
qa.a: Let her keep practising her brother's turn-and-sit with someone nearby, and show the steps slowly so she can copy them more closely.

qa.q: How might her brother feel if he saw her copy him?
qa.a: He might feel proud and amused to be copied by his little sister.

grounding: A visitor's note records a toddler loosely copying her older brother's turn-sit-swing climb and landing closer than before.

passage: After lunch in the house near Kolhapur, Manoj dropped onto the old sofa the way he always did: turned round, sat, swung his legs up. Jyoti, on the floor, stared. She stood, turned in a wobbly circle, pressed her bottom to the seat edge and kicked one leg high. She ended up hanging over the cushion, halfway on. "Look, Aai!" Manoj laughed. "She's copying me!" Jyoti pulled herself further, grinning.

qa.q: Who laughed when Jyoti copied him?
qa.a: Manoj laughed.

qa.q: What was Jyoti thinking as she turned in a wobbly circle?
qa.a: She seemed determined and excited, trying to do exactly what Manoj did.

qa.q: What else could help Jyoti get all the way up?
qa.a: Manoj could do the moves slowly beside her, so she sees each step clearly.

qa.q: How does Manoj feel about being copied?
qa.a: He is delighted and proud, calling to Aai to look.

grounding: A toddler copies her older brother's way of climbing the sofa and lands halfway on, closer than before.

passage:
"Up!" Yusuf stood facing the sofa, both arms stretched high.
"Again?" Abba looked over his newspaper.
"Up! Up!"
Zainab, his sister, snorted. "He can climb, Abba. I've seen him."
"Up!" Yusuf bounced on his toes, arms still reaching.
Abba folded the paper, scooped Yusuf under the arms and set him on the seat.
Yusuf patted the cushion, satisfied. "Up."

qa.q: What was Abba reading?
qa.a: He was reading a newspaper.

qa.q: How can you tell Yusuf felt satisfied at the end?
qa.a: He patted the cushion and said "Up" calmly, as if his plan had worked perfectly.

qa.q: What would you change if Abba wants Yusuf to try more himself?
qa.a: Abba could stand beside him and give a knee or a hand to push on, so Yusuf does part of the climb.

qa.q: How does Zainab see Yusuf's plan?
qa.a: Zainab thinks it's a bit lazy because she knows he can climb, so she is amused and a little annoyed.

grounding: A toddler lifts both arms and says "up" so his father lifts him onto the sofa and no climbing is needed.

passage:
Babysitting note, Friday evening
When Parul's father came home, Parul went to the sofa, stood facing it, raised both arms high and said, "Up." He lifted her onto the seat. Earlier, with me, she had climbed it herself using a knee. She only asks with her arms when her father is in the room. I mentioned this to him; he said he enjoys lifting her.

qa.q: What did Parul say when she raised her arms?
qa.a: She said, "Up."

qa.q: What might Parul be wanting when she raises her arms to her father?
qa.a: She seems to want closeness and comfort with him, and feels confident he will lift her.

qa.q: What else could the family try so Parul keeps her climbing skill?
qa.a: Her father could sometimes stand close and let her climb with a knee, and lift her other times, so both ways stay open.

qa.q: How does Parul's father feel about the lifting?
qa.a: He enjoys lifting her, as he said himself.

grounding: A babysitter's note records a toddler raising her arms and saying "up" so her father lifts her, making climbing unnecessary.

passage:
"Watch, Francis mama," Bhupen's mother said. "Bhupen, show him."
Bhupen marched to the sofa, planted a knee on the seat's edge and pushed. Up.
"Wah!" said Francis mama. "How did he learn that?"
"Last week the knee worked once. Now it's always the knee."
"Down, and again!" Bhupen slid off, knee up, push. Up. Faster than before.
"He's timing himself," Francis mama laughed.

qa.q: What did Bhupen plant on the seat's edge?
qa.a: He planted a knee on the seat's edge.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling as he slid off to go again?
qa.a: He was proud and excited, eager to show off his fast climb.

qa.q: What else could Bhupen's mother try to keep him learning?
qa.a: She could offer a different sofa or a higher chair with her nearby, so he tests whether the knee trick works elsewhere.

qa.q: How does Francis mama see the climbing?
qa.a: He is impressed and amused, laughing that Bhupen seems to be timing himself.

grounding: A toddler starts every sofa climb with the knee that worked before and gets faster each time.

passage:
Crèche note, Monday
Pankaj has found his way onto the reading couch. Last Friday he got up by pressing one knee on the couch's front edge. Today, every time, he began the same way: knee first, push, roll in. By the fourth time he was up in a few seconds. His father, Santosh, arrived at pickup and watched him do it twice, smiling. I stood beside the couch each time.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do first every time today?
qa.a: He began the same way: knee first, push, roll in.

qa.q: How can you tell Pankaj felt confident?
qa.a: He climbed straight up every time without hesitating and got faster, by the fourth time taking only a few seconds.

qa.q: What small step could the note-writer try next?
qa.a: They could offer a slightly different couch or step with them standing beside it, so Pankaj practises adapting his knee move.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel watching?
qa.a: Santosh seems pleased and proud, smiling as he watches his son climb twice.

grounding: A crèche note records a toddler who repeats the knee-first climb that worked before and gets faster each time.

passage: I'm Vaibhav, Darshan's cousin, and I was there on Diwali when it happened. Darshan saw the sweets on the sofa and ran at it, not at the low seat but at the tall wooden armrest. He grabbed the top, kicked, and his foot slid on the polish. Dadi, sitting right there, caught him under the arms before he hit the floor. He laughed. My heart was still banging.

qa.q: Who caught Darshan?
qa.a: Dadi caught him under the arms.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling after Darshan slipped?
qa.a: Vaibhav was frightened and shaken, heart still banging after the near fall.

qa.q: What else could have made Darshan's climb safer?
qa.a: Putting the sweets somewhere else and showing him the low seat, since he rushed at the tallest part without checking.

qa.q: What was the slip probably like for Darshan?
qa.a: For Darshan it was probably exciting and fun, since he laughed after being caught.

grounding: An observer describes a toddler who rushes at a tall armrest instead of the seat, slips and is caught by a grandparent.

passage:
Sunday: Gurleen spotted her doll on the sofa and raced to the high armrest, not the seat. Her hands slipped and Biji caught her.
Wednesday: she went at the armrest again. Biji stood close, turned her gently to the low seat and said, "Here, puttar."
Friday: when Rukmini aunty visited, Gurleen headed toward the armrest, stopped, looked at Biji, and went round to the seat.

qa.q: What did Biji say on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said, "Here, puttar."

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she raced to the armrest on Sunday?
qa.a: She was excited to reach her doll and not at all worried about slipping.

qa.q: What helped change Gurleen's climbing, and why?
qa.a: Biji stayed close and turned her toward the low seat, giving her a safer spot to copy.

qa.q: How might Rukmini aunty see Gurleen's pause?
qa.a: Rukmini aunty might see a small child stopping to check, which looks thoughtful for her age.

grounding: Over several days a toddler who rushed at the tall armrest and slipped is caught and guided by her grandmother toward the safer seat.

passage:
"Ow!" Jasleen slid off the sofa edge and bumped down onto the rug.
"Oh, sweetheart," Avni said, reaching for her. "You okay?"
Jasleen twisted away, crying, and jumped at the same corner. Slip. Down again.
"Jassu, wait..."
"No!" Another jump, the same way. Slip.
"Maybe try the middle?"
Jasleen sobbed louder and jumped again.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen bump down?
qa.a: She bumped down onto the rug.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling as she jumped again and again?
qa.a: She was angry and upset, too frustrated to stop and change anything.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Jasleen?
qa.a: Help her calm down first, perhaps with a hug or a pause, so she can then try a new spot like the middle.

qa.q: How does Jasleen's repeated jumping feel for Avni?
qa.a: Avni wants to help and suggests trying the middle, but her ideas are pushed away, which is hard.

grounding: After slipping, a toddler cries but keeps jumping at the same spot in the same way, and each attempt fails.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday
Vaibhav slipped off the soft couch this morning and cried. Then, still crying, he jumped at the same corner in the very same way, three more times. He slipped each time. I sat by him and said, "That was hard," until he stopped crying. Then I tapped the lower middle part. He tried there and got a knee up. His mother, Manjula, will hear the full story at pickup.

qa.q: How many more times did Vaibhav jump at the same corner?
qa.a: He jumped three more times.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he kept jumping at the corner?
qa.a: He was upset and frustrated, crying and too stuck to try something new.

qa.q: What worked here, and why?
qa.a: Calming him first and then tapping the lower middle part, because once he stopped crying he could try a different spot.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel hearing the story?
qa.a: Manjula would likely feel sympathetic that he struggled and glad someone helped him calm down and try again.

grounding: A daycare note describes a toddler repeating the same failing jump after slipping, until an adult helps him pause and change spot.
